Something above him moved . The weight across his torso dipped, then ground slightly sideways, a low, gravelly slide that pressed new pain into his legs and kicked up another burst of dust. He froze. A larger block near his head scraped down half an inch with a lazy, predatory shrug. Instinct took over before thought could catch up — his left arm snapped upward, wedging between the stone and his face. Not to shove it back — he didn’t have that kind of leverage — but just to catch it. Slow it. Redirect it. If it came down further, it was going to hit something. Better the arm than the eye. The last dust stirred loose by the shift hit his lungs like sandpaper. He choked, sharp and sudden, and the cough tore through his body before he could stop it. Stone dug deeper into his side as his ribs convulsed, and a fresh spray of pebbles tumbled down his collarbone — dry, biting, unkind. Above him, the ceiling of stone responded. It shifted again. Just once. Then — mercifully — it stopped. His chest heaved, but he forced it smaller. Slower. Every breath was an act of balance now. Too deep, and the rubble pressed down. Too shallow, and he’d choke on the dust still clinging to his throat. He was awake now. Fully. No more haze. No more drifting thoughts. Just the weight. The dust. The sound of his own pulse in his ears. If he moved too much, the whole pile would remember what it was capable of. Every breath shifted the stones by fractions. Every shift tempted gravity to finish the job. The Eyrie hadn’t just collapsed. It had buried him. And all he could do — the only thing — was stay very, very still... ...and hope the next person to find him wasn’t the seven-foot steroid golem that put him here in the first place. Ch 2 – Liminal David didn’t know if he’d blacked out again, or if time had just slithered sideways without telling him. There was no sky to track. No light to shift. Just the weight, the ache, and the slow, dry scrape of dust collecting in his lungs with every shallow breath. Random pains seemed to shift or bloom when he hadn’t been paying attention. His right arm was still a blank in his perception. Maybe asleep. Maybe broken. Hard to say. Harder to care. It wasn’t coming back online anytime soon either way. His left was another story. That one still worked, still braced above him, still bearing the load. His forearm wedged between his face and the nearest stone, keeping it from finishing the job. The muscles in his shoulder screamed now — not in bursts, but in a steady, smoldering burn, like fire left to smother under its own ash. A pain too quiet to scream, too loud to ignore. He hadn’t dared move it. Not for... minutes? Hours? He had taken to resting its weight against his forehead, but the pressure of the stones above still kept the muscle tight. However long it had been, the limb was shaking now. Not much. Just the tiniest tremble. But in a place like this, tiny had teeth. At some point, he started hearing things. A voice? Maybe. Probably not. Prolonged silence did weird things to a person’s mind, and with this headache, it was likely just his own thoughts bouncing off him. No, that wasn’t it... it was more of a yell. Far off. Muffled. Familiar in a way that made his chest seize up for reasons he couldn’t quite name. Was that him, or something real? He held his breath, forcing himself to listen through the roar of his own pulse. There. Something again. Footsteps? The crunch of sand under boots? Soft voices filtered in through the silence — so faint he almost missed them. “Why is he chasing her like that?” “Because it’s Jill. Nemesis sees that uniform and gets tunnel vision. I’d be shocked if he wasn’t chasing her.” “So, then we... what? Just let her get chased?” “Well yeah. She’ll be ok. We can get things done in the meantime.” David blinked slowly, grit dragging across his lashes. He hadn’t imagined it. Someone was out there. Outside the Eyrie. Getting closer . It was surreal. Voices drifting past like it was just another day in the Fog, laughing about killer patterns and survivor bait while he lay crushed in the dark, half-buried under a structure that wanted to finish folding him like a lawn chair. His sanity creaked under the weight of it. A small prickle of panic clawed at the back of his throat. He couldn’t tell where the voices were coming from just from the sound alone — whether they were near the Eyrie or just passing by . He couldn’t wave. Couldn’t even shift enough to make noise without risking a full cave-in. But if they didn’t come into the building... if they didn’t see the rubble... They’d miss him entirely. He didn’t have the luxury of waiting. He had to try. He swallowed. The grit in his throat made the motion grind. He tried to shout. Nothing. A wheeze. A cough. Pain flared in his ribs as a stone shifted threateningly and jabbed his side. “Here,” he rasped, a thread of voice scraping out like broken glass. “Hey—!” It wasn’t much. Just two syllables and a thread of panic. But they scratched their way through the cracks. And Dwight stopped walking. Mid-step. Boot still half-hovering over the sand. “...Wait.” Felix paused beside him, glancing back. “What is it?” “I — hold on.” Dwight tilted his head, gaze flicking toward the building. “I thought I heard something.” Felix didn’t catch it, whatever it was.
